section.title: The Fall of Samaria
section.sectionRationale: After Hoshea's failed rebellion, Assyria conquers Samaria and exiles the northern kingdom permanently. The chapter pauses the narrative to give the author's own extended theological verdict on why Israel fell, tracing two and a half centuries of persistent idolatry back to the golden calves, then describes the mixed, syncretistic worship of the foreign peoples resettled in Israel's place.
section.thesis: The fall of the northern kingdom was not an accident of geopolitics but the LORD's just and long-warned judgment on centuries of covenant unfaithfulness, a verdict so decisive that even the pagan settlers who replace Israel inherit a warning about worshiping the LORD alongside other gods.
section.frameNote: Four beats: Hoshea's reign and Samaria's fall, verses 1 to 6; the author's extended theological explanation of Israel's sin, verses 7 to 23; the resettlement of Samaria by foreign peoples, verses 24 to 34; and the LORD's covenant demand for exclusive worship, verses 35 to 41.

units.label: Hoshea's reign and Samaria's fall
units.note: the king of Assyria captured Samaria

verses.text: In the twelfth year of the reign of Ahaz over Judah, Hoshea son of Elah became king of Israel, and he reigned in Samaria nine years.
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, but not like the kings of Israel who preceded him.
Shalmaneser king of Assyria attacked him, and Hoshea became his vassal and paid him tribute.

But the king of Assyria discovered that Hoshea had conspired to send envoys to King So of Egypt, and that he had not paid tribute to the king of Assyria as in previous years. Therefore the king of Assyria arrested Hoshea and put him in prison.
Then the king of Assyria invaded the whole land, marched up to Samaria, and besieged it for three years.

In the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of Assyria captured Samaria and carried away the Israelites to Assyria, where he settled them in Halah, in Gozan by the Habor River, and in the cities of the Medes.

All this happened because the people of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt from under the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt. They had worshiped other gods
and walked in the customs of the nations that the LORD had driven out before the Israelites, as well as in the practices introduced by the kings of Israel.
The Israelites secretly did things against the LORD their God that were not right. From watchtower to fortified city, they built high places in all their cities.
They set up for themselves sacred pillars and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every green tree.
They burned incense on all the high places like the nations that the LORD had driven out before them. They did wicked things, provoking the LORD to anger.
They served {{pesel|idols}}, although the LORD had told them, "You shall not do this thing."

Yet through all His prophets and seers, the LORD warned Israel and Judah, saying, "Turn from your wicked ways and keep My commandments and statutes, according to the entire Law that I commanded your fathers and delivered to you through My servants the prophets."
But they would not listen, and they stiffened their {{oref|necks}} like their fathers, who did not believe the LORD their God.

They rejected His statutes and the covenant He had made with their fathers, as well as the decrees He had given them. They pursued worthless idols and became worthless themselves, going after the surrounding nations that the LORD had commanded them not to imitate.
They abandoned all the commandments of the LORD their God and made for themselves two cast idols of calves and an Asherah pole. They bowed down to all the host of heaven and served Baal.
They sacrificed their sons and daughters in the fire and practiced divination and soothsaying. They devoted themselves to doing evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking Him to anger.
So the LORD was very angry with Israel, and He removed them from His presence. Only the tribe of Judah remained,
and even Judah did not keep the commandments of the LORD their God, but lived according to the customs Israel had introduced.
So the LORD rejected all the descendants of Israel. He afflicted them and delivered them into the hands of plunderers, until He had banished them from His presence.
When the LORD had torn Israel away from the house of David, they made Jeroboam son of Nebat king, and Jeroboam led Israel away from following the LORD and caused them to commit a great sin.
The Israelites persisted in all the sins that Jeroboam had committed and did not turn away from them.

Finally, the LORD removed Israel from His presence, as He had declared through all His servants the prophets. So Israel was {{galah|exiled}} from their homeland into Assyria, where they are to this day.

units.label: Foreign peoples resettle Samaria
units.note: the LORD sent lions among them

verses.text: Then the king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim and settled them in the towns of Samaria to replace the Israelites. They took possession of Samaria and lived in its towns.
Now when the settlers first lived there, they did not worship the LORD, so He sent lions among them, which killed some of them.

So they spoke to the king of Assyria, saying, "The peoples that you have removed and placed in the cities of Samaria do not know the requirements of the God of the land. Because of this, He has sent lions among them, which are indeed killing them off."
Then the king of Assyria commanded: "Send back one of the priests you carried off from Samaria, and have him go back to live there and teach the requirements of the God of the land."
Thus one of the priests they had carried away came and lived in Bethel, and he began to teach them how they should worship the LORD.

Nevertheless, the people of each nation continued to make their own gods in the cities where they had settled, and they set them up in the shrines that the people of Samaria had made on the high places.
The men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth, the men of Cuth made Nergal, the men of Hamath made Ashima,
the Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burned their children in the fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech the gods of Sepharvaim.
So the new residents worshiped the LORD, but they also appointed for themselves priests of all sorts to serve in the shrines of the high places.
They worshiped the LORD, but they also served their own gods according to the customs of the nations from which they had been carried away.

To this day they are still practicing their former customs. None of them worship the LORD or observe the statutes, ordinances, laws, and commandments that the LORD gave the descendants of Jacob, whom He named Israel.

units.label: The covenant demand for exclusive worship

verses.text: For the LORD had made a covenant with the Israelites and commanded them, "Do not {{yare|worship}} other gods or bow down to them; do not serve them or sacrifice to them.
Instead, worship the LORD, who brought you out of the land of Egypt with great power and an outstretched arm. You are to bow down to Him and offer sacrifices to Him.
And you must always be careful to observe the statutes, ordinances, laws, and commandments He wrote for you. Do not worship other gods.
Do not forget the covenant I have made with you. Do not worship other gods,
but worship the LORD your God, and He will deliver you from the hands of all your enemies."
But they would not listen, and they persisted in their former customs.
So these nations worshiped the LORD but also served their idols, and to this day their children and grandchildren continue to do as their fathers did.

pesel.gloss: A carved or cast idol, explicitly forbidden by the second commandment, Exodus 20:4. That Israel served pesel after the LORD had specifically said, you shall not do this thing, underscores that their judgment came not from ignorance of God's will but from willful, repeated defiance of a command they knew perfectly well.

oref.gloss: Neck, used idiomatically for stubborn resistance, to stiffen the oref meaning to refuse correction like an animal that will not be led. The same phrase describes Israel at Sinai, Exodus 32:9, showing this final judgment answers a pattern of resistance that had characterized the nation from its very beginning.

galah.gloss: To uncover, remove, or go into exile. This is the pivotal word of the entire book, marking the fulfillment of the covenant curse threatened in Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28, and setting the trajectory that Judah itself will follow in 2 Kings 25 when it, too, is finally exiled from the land.

yare.gloss: To fear, revere, or worship, though the BSB here renders it worship in the specific sense of reverent submission owed exclusively to the LORD. The covenant repeatedly commands Israel not to yare other gods but to reserve this reverence entirely for the LORD who redeemed them from Egypt, the very command generations of kings and people alike refused to keep.

basic.context: Hoshea, Israel's last king, rebels against Assyria by seeking Egyptian help and withholding tribute, prompting a three-year siege that ends with Samaria's capture and the permanent exile of the northern kingdom's population. The author pauses the narrative here to deliver an extended theological verdict, tracing Israel's fall not to bad luck or weak politics but to over two centuries of persistent idolatry, beginning with Jeroboam's golden calves and continuing despite repeated prophetic warnings, until the LORD finally removed Israel from His presence exactly as He had declared. The chapter closes by describing the mixed, syncretistic worship of the foreign peoples Assyria resettled in Israel's place, who worshiped the LORD alongside their own gods, and by restating the covenant's original demand for Israel's exclusive worship of the LORD alone.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative combined with the author's own inspired theological commentary explaining the meaning of the events just narrated; it functions as the interpretive key for the entire book of Kings. What endures is the sober truth that persistent, unrepented covenant unfaithfulness brings real historical consequences, and that partial or mixed worship, giving the LORD some allegiance alongside other loyalties, ultimately fails to honor Him as He requires.
basic.originalLanguages: Israel served pesel, carved idols, in direct defiance of a command they clearly knew, and stiffened their oref, neck, refusing correction exactly as their ancestors had at Sinai. The result is galah, exile, the pivotal covenant curse now fully realized and destined to fall on Judah as well in the book's final chapters. And the covenant's repeated demand that Israel yare, worship or revere, the LORD exclusively, rather than alongside other gods, frames the entire chapter's verdict on both Israel's fall and the resettled peoples' incomplete devotion.
basic.typology: Israel's persistent, willful covenant unfaithfulness culminating in exile previews humanity's own persistent rebellion against God despite repeated warning, while the demand for wholehearted, exclusive worship anticipates the New Testament's insistence that no one can serve two masters, a truth fulfilled perfectly only in Christ's undivided devotion to the Father.
basic.christ: The prophets sent again and again to call wayward Israel back before judgment fell anticipates the ultimate Prophet, Jesus Christ, who likewise came to His own people with a final and greater call to repentance, Matthew 23:37-38, and whose rejection, like the prophets before Him, still did not exhaust God's patience but led instead to the offer of salvation extended to all nations, exactly as the exile scattered Israel yet ultimately served God's larger redemptive purposes.
basic.god: God is patient, sending prophet after prophet across centuries before finally executing the judgment He had long warned of, showing that His judgment, however severe, is neither impulsive nor unjust but the fitting response to sustained, willful rebellion. He is also exclusively jealous, refusing to share worship with any other god, a demand rooted not in pettiness but in His unique identity as the one true God who alone redeemed Israel from Egypt.
basic.crossReferences: Leviticus 26:27-33 and Deuteronomy 28:36-37, 64 foretold precisely this exile centuries in advance, showing the LORD's word, not mere political circumstance, governed Israel's fall. Exodus 32:9 first describes Israel as stiff-necked at Sinai, the same charge repeated here at the end of the northern kingdom's history. Matthew 6:24 teaches that no one can serve two masters, directly addressing the mixed worship the resettled peoples practice at this chapter's close.
basic.oneStory: This chapter is the theological hinge of the entire book of Kings, explaining in the author's own voice why Israel fell: not political misfortune but centuries of willful covenant unfaithfulness met, at last, by God's long-threatened and perfectly just judgment, a pattern that will soon overtake Judah as well and that finds its ultimate resolution only in Christ, whose perfect, undivided devotion to the Father succeeds where Israel and every mixed-worship nation after it had failed.

context.literary: The chapter is built as two matching panels of roughly equal weight, framed by an unusually long editorial voice. Verses 1 to 6 narrate Hoshea's reign and Samaria's fall in plain historical prose, six verses covering nine years and a three year siege. Verses 7 to 23 then stop the clock entirely: the narrator steps forward in his own voice to explain the meaning of what has just happened, the longest single piece of theological commentary anywhere in the book of Kings. That commentary is framed by a deliberate repetition of its key verb: it opens by saying the LORD removed them from His presence, verse 18, and closes by saying the LORD removed Israel from their homeland, verse 23, the same verb, removed, applied first to a relationship and finally to a place, as though the geographical exile of verse 23 is simply the theological exile of verse 18 finally worked out into space and history. Inside that frame, the catalogue of sins in verses 9 to 17 escalates deliberately, moving from secret, covert practice, to open high places on every hill, to specific named idolatries, to astral worship, and finally to child sacrifice, the same horror just committed by Judah's own king two chapters earlier, so that the worst sin named for Israel and the worst sin already shown for Ahaz turn out to be identical. Verses 24 to 41 then form a second panel that mirrors the first's structure, a fresh population arriving, learning imperfectly, and settling into the same divided worship pattern the first panel just spent seventeen verses condemning, so that the chapter ends nearly where it began, with people who do not truly know the LORD living in the land He gave to a people who once did.
context.historical: Sargon II's own royal inscriptions, discovered at Khorsabad, claim credit for completing Samaria's capture and record deporting tens of thousands of its people, a report consistent with, though independent of, this chapter's account; the siege itself likely began under Shalmaneser V, verse 3, who may have died before the city actually fell, with Sargon then claiming the conquest as his own, a common feature of Assyrian royal rhetoric. The specific resettlement described in verse 24, people brought from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim, names real Mesopotamian and Syrian cities rather than a vague elsewhere, matching Assyria's documented policy of transplanting whole populations to break local identity and prevent renewed rebellion, the same strategy already used on Israel itself. The destinations named for the exiled Israelites in verse 6, Halah, Gozan on the Habor River, and the cities of the Medes, are attested Assyrian provincial regions, and 1 Chronicles 5:26 places an earlier wave of Transjordanian exiles in the identical locations under the same Assyrian king, showing this deportation was the culmination of a policy already decades old by the time Samaria fell. The returning priest of verses 27 to 28, sent back specifically to teach the requirements of the God of the land, reflects a genuinely attested ancient assumption, that each territory answered to its own deity, whose favor a wise occupying power would want restored rather than risk; Assyria's response to the lions is thus not evidence of respect for the LORD's uniqueness but of a pragmatic policy toward any local god thought capable of causing harm.
context.canonical: Israel's calf worship traces back, by this chapter's own account, to one founding decision, Jeroboam's two golden calves, first built at 1 Kings 12:28 with the words Here, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt, deliberately echoing the exodus formula in order to hijack it. Two centuries later, on the very eve of this fall, the prophet Hosea mocks the same object in almost identical terms, He has rejected your calf, O Samaria, it will be broken to pieces, that calf of Samaria, Hosea 8:5-6, showing this chapter's verdict was not written after the fact by a distant historian but was already being preached, unheeded, by a contemporary prophet as the walls of Samaria still stood. The chapter's forward reach is just as striking. Its picture of a mixed population that worshiped the LORD but also served their idols, verse 41, becomes the historical seedbed for the Samaritans the Gospels later describe, whose incomplete worship Jesus diagnoses directly, you worship what you do not know, John 4:22, before announcing that true worship will no longer depend on any mountain or temple at all. What this chapter records as judgment on a mixed, half-taught people, the Gospels and Acts eventually record as a mission field: the same Samaria that could not worship rightly here becomes, centuries later, the first territory outside Jerusalem to receive the gospel and the Spirit, Acts 8:14-17.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The historian writes to forestall a very natural but false inference, that Israel fell because Assyria's gods proved stronger than the LORD. Verse 7 heads off that reading before any military detail is given, stating flatly that all this happened because the people of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God, making Israel's own covenant unfaithfulness, not Assyrian military superiority, the operative cause. He intends his audience, quite plausibly Judahites living through or anticipating their own catastrophe, to recognize that defeat by a pagan empire is not proof of divine weakness but can be, and here specifically is, proof of divine justice long delayed. He also intends the reader to feel the weight of verse 13's claim that warning came through all His prophets and seers across generations, not as a single missed chance but as centuries of patiently offered correction refused every time, so that when judgment finally lands it cannot be read as impulsive, disproportionate, or a departure from anything God had not already promised in the covenant curses of Deuteronomy and Leviticus long before any king of Israel was born.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The chapter's closing note, to this day, repeated in verses 23, 34, and 41, marks the author's own later vantage point looking back on decades or centuries of continued syncretism; it describes an observed, ongoing condition rather than prescribing a new rule for how future readers must worship. What functions as binding instruction is not new at all: verses 35 to 39 simply restate covenant stipulations already given at Sinai, quoted almost verbatim, so that the chapter's demand for exclusive worship carries force not because this narrator invents it here but because it was already law. Applied today, the chapter does not suggest that mixed worship communities should be regarded as outside all hope of instruction, since a priest is in fact sent to teach the new residents, however incompletely that teaching succeeds; it does insist that partial, divided devotion, God included alongside other final loyalties, never counts as the covenant faithfulness the LORD actually requires.

debates.question: How should the mixed worship of the resettled peoples, verses 24 to 41, be assessed, given that they did, in some sense, worship the LORD?

views.label: Genuinely condemned as no true worship at all
views.case: The passage states plainly, in verse 41, that these peoples worshiped the LORD but also served their idols, and verse 33 says essentially the same thing, that they worshiped the LORD but they also served their own gods, and verse 34 concludes bluntly that none of them truly worship the LORD; including the LORD alongside other gods does not soften the verdict but seals it, since the covenant demand restated at length in verses 35 to 39 leaves no room for shared devotion.

views.label: An early, partially instructed stage that later developed further
views.case: A priest is specifically sent back to teach them how they should worship the LORD, verse 28, implying a genuine, if incomplete, process of instruction was underway rather than a fixed, final verdict; the descendants of this same population, the Samaritans, retain a real if theologically thin connection to worship of Israel's God centuries later, acknowledged even by Jesus, John 4:20-22.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree the text explicitly denies that divided devotion counts as covenant faithfulness; they differ on whether that denial describes a permanently fixed condition or an early stage in a longer, still unfinished story that the Gospels eventually pick back up.

debates.question: Does the chapter trace Israel's fall to one founding sin, Jeroboam's calves, or to the accumulated weight of two centuries of separate offenses?

views.label: One founding sin set the whole course
views.case: Verses 21 to 22 single out the moment the LORD had torn Israel away from the house of David and made Jeroboam king, naming the great sin he caused Israel to commit as the specific cause the Israelites persisted in and did not turn away from, treating the calves as the headwater every later corruption flowed from.

views.label: A long accumulation across many kings
views.case: Verses 7 to 17 catalogue an extensive range of separate offenses, secret sins, high places on every hill, sacred pillars, Asherah poles, astral worship, divination, and finally child sacrifice, a list far too broad to be explained by one founding decision alone, suggesting two centuries of kings each adding their own layer to a compounding pattern.

debates.bearing: The text itself holds both together: it keeps returning to Jeroboam by name as the paradigm case even while cataloguing sins that clearly outgrew anything one king alone could have introduced, showing a founding compromise that metastasized rather than one that stayed contained.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond pesel, oref, galah, and yare already carried in this study's lexicon, several more details in the Hebrew sharpen the indictment. Verse 16's host of heaven, tseva hashamayim, names the sun, moon, and stars gathered under a single word, tseva, that elsewhere simply means an army; Israel is charged with bowing to the very lights God arrayed like a marshaled host, Deuteronomy 4:19, exchanging worship of their commander for worship of his troops.

The Asherah pole of verse 16 transliterates a Canaanite goddess's own name into a wooden cult object set up in her honor; Deuteronomy 16:21 forbids planting any such pole next to the altar you will build for the LORD your God, meaning the sin here is not merely idolatry in the abstract but the specific, deliberate placement of a rival symbol immediately beside the LORD's own worship site, blurring the two by proximity rather than open replacement.

The sacred pillars, matstsebah, in verse 10 name an object whose form is not inherently evil; the same word describes the stone Jacob sets up and calls Bethel, Genesis 28:18, a legitimate memorial to a true encounter with God. By Deuteronomy's time the same physical object, set up as a fixture of ongoing worship rather than a one time memorial, has become something the LORD your God hates, Deuteronomy 16:22, showing that intent and use, not shape alone, determine whether a stone honors God or competes with Him.

Verse 15 turns on a pointed wordplay easy to miss in translation: Israel pursued worthless idols and became worthless themselves, both instances translating hevel, the same word Ecclesiastes repeats as vanity of vanities. The Hebrew does not merely say idols are empty; it says worshipers become as empty as what they worship, a transformation rather than a mere association. Jeremiah later uses nearly identical wording of the whole nation, they followed worthless idols, and became worthless themselves, Jeremiah 2:5, showing this chapter's diagnosis of Israel was already a settled prophetic formula rather than one historian's own invention.

Finally, verse 9's claim that Israel secretly did things against the LORD pictures sin hidden under the appearance of ordinary civic life, from watchtower to fortified city, as though every level of settlement, from the smallest outpost to the strongest wall, concealed the same rot behind its normal function.

typology.type: Centuries of warning refused, met at last by decisive judgment
typology.fulfillment: Verse 13 pictures the LORD sending all His prophets and seers across generations before finally removing Israel from His presence, verse 23, patience that runs for centuries before judgment falls. The pattern recurs and intensifies with Israel's own Messiah, how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling, Matthew 23:37, spoken over Jerusalem shortly before its own later fall. Where the northern kingdom's rejected warnings ended only in exile, the rejection of the greater Prophet ends in a cross that itself becomes, unlike Samaria's fall, the very means of the world's rescue.

typology.type: Worship divided between the LORD and other gods, denied the name of true worship
typology.fulfillment: Verse 41 states plainly that the resettled peoples worshiped the LORD but also served their idols, echoing verse 33's report that they worshiped the LORD but they also served their own gods, and verse 34 refuses to count this as worship of the LORD at all. Christ states the same principle as an absolute, no one can serve two masters, you cannot serve both God and money, Matthew 6:24. What this chapter treats as a scandal peculiar to conquered pagans, the Gospel treats as a universal temptation, and only Christ Himself, tested in every way yet undivided in obedience to His Father, Hebrews 4:15, ever meets the standard perfectly.

typology.type: A remnant preserved when the wider nation is removed
typology.fulfillment: Only the tribe of Judah remained, verse 18, a single surviving thread kept intact while the rest of the nation is carried away. Paul later names this pattern explicitly as still operating in his own day, at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace, Romans 11:5, tracing a line of preserved faithfulness through judgment that runs from this very moment forward into the church. The remnant here is small, one tribe out of twelve, but it is enough, because it is the tribe carrying the promise to David that will not fail.

typology.type: An exiled priest sent back to teach a people who do not yet know the LORD
typology.fulfillment: One of Israel's own deported priests is sent home specifically to teach them how they should worship the LORD, verse 28, though the teaching only partly succeeds, verse 33. Centuries later, another teacher meets a woman from this same region at a well and tells her plainly, you worship what you do not know, before promising that the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth, John 4:22-24. The incomplete instruction this chapter records finds its completion not in a returned priest but in the one greater than any priest, met at Jacob's well in the very territory this chapter describes.

study.christ:
This chapter's christological weight falls chiefly on three threads already gathered in its typology, drawn together here. The centuries of ignored prophets culminate, on the far side of two more exiles, in the Prophet Israel's leaders finally reject outright, O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling, Matthew 23:37. The grief in that lament answers this chapter's own account of patient, repeated warning; the same God who kept sending seers to a stiff-necked Israel keeps sending, finally sending His own Son, to a Jerusalem that treats Him no better than Samaria treated the prophets who called it back before it fell.

The chapter's insistence that divided worship is no true worship at all, verses 33 to 34, anticipates Christ's own flat refusal to divide devotion between God and any rival, you cannot serve both God and money, Matthew 6:24, a command He does not merely teach but lives, undivided in obedience even under the full weight of temptation, Hebrews 4:15. Where the resettled peoples of this chapter could not manage undivided devotion even with a priest sent to instruct them, Christ manages it perfectly with no instruction needed, being Himself the instruction.

Most strikingly, this chapter's tragic conclusion, that none of these peoples worship the LORD rightly, verse 34, finds its narrative answer four Gospels and one book of Acts later in the very same territory. The Samaritan woman Jesus meets is told plainly that she and her people worship what you do not know, yet she is also told that a time has arrived when true worship no longer depends on Jerusalem's temple at all, John 4:21-24. What this chapter could only diagnose as failure, the New Testament resolves as fulfillment: Samaria, once judged for worship it never fully understood, becomes in Acts 8 the first territory outside Judea to receive the gospel and the Holy Spirit, proof that the God who removed Israel from His presence in this chapter is the same God who, in Christ, draws even Samaria back into it.
study.god:
Two attributes hold this chapter in tension without either one canceling the other. God is patient almost past reckoning: verse 13 pictures Him sending all His prophets and seers across roughly two centuries of the northern kingdom's existence, never striking without first warning, never warning only once. And God is exclusively jealous for His people's worship, a demand restated at length in verses 35 to 39, do not worship other gods, worship the LORD your God, repeated across five verses as though the point cannot be made too plainly. These two attributes are not competitors; the patience is precisely what makes the eventual judgment just rather than arbitrary, since it comes only after every avenue of warning has been exhausted, and the jealousy is precisely what makes the patience meaningful, since a God indifferent to shared worship would have no reason to keep sending prophets to prevent it.

The chapter also reveals God's sovereignty over the very empire that seems to defeat Him. Assyria's conquest looks, to any observer unfamiliar with Israel's God, like proof that Assyria's gods outperformed the LORD; the narrator refuses that reading outright, insisting the entire catastrophe unfolded because the people of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God, verse 7, meaning Assyria functioned as an instrument of a purpose it did not itself choose or understand, a sovereignty this book's own prophetic partner will make explicit later, Assyria, the rod of My anger, Isaiah 10:5.

Finally, God's presence itself is shown to be something that can, in real historical fact, be withdrawn: the chapter twice says He removed them from His presence, verses 18 and 23, the same phrase framing the whole theological unit. This is not a metaphor drained of weight; a nation once given land, king, and temple is now given none of these, a genuine loss of nearness that makes the later promise of a remnant restored, and eventually a whole world reconciled to that presence in Christ, something worth the fullest possible weight of gratitude rather than casual assumption.

crossReferences.note: Foretells centuries in advance the exact exile and scattering that befalls Israel in this chapter, land laid waste and cities left in ruins, showing that God's own word, not mere Assyrian circumstance or Israel's weak politics, actually governed how this catastrophe unfolded.

Foretells that the LORD will scatter you among all the nations to worship gods of wood and stone, precisely the divided, wood and stone worship this chapter records both for exiled Israel and for the peoples who replace them, showing the curse and its outworking match closely.

Describes Israel already resisting Moses at Sinai in this exact language, generations before Samaria ever existed, so that the resistance judged here was never a sudden departure but the same posture carried unbroken across centuries of prophetic warning and royal example.

Records Jeroboam's founding words over the two golden calves, Here, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt, the same exodus language twisted from the start, and the specific great sin this chapter blames for Israel's entire subsequent history, verses 21 to 22.

A contemporary prophet mocks the same calf this chapter condemns, He has rejected your calf, O Samaria, it will be broken to pieces, preached, apparently unheeded, while the kingdom Hosea addressed was still standing, showing this chapter's verdict was already being spoken aloud before the walls fell.

Records an earlier deportation of the Transjordanian tribes to the identical region, Halah, Habor, and the river of Gozan, under the same Assyrian king, showing this chapter's exile completed a policy already decades old rather than a single isolated catastrophe.

Commands, fear the LORD your God, serve Him only, the very covenant demand restated at length in verses 35 to 39 and quoted directly by Christ Himself when tempted to worship any power but His Father, Luke 4:8.

Christ's teaching that no one can serve two masters directly addresses the mixed, divided worship condemned throughout the closing verses of this chapter, a devotion split between the LORD and rival gods that this chapter refuses to count as worship at all.

Jesus meets a woman from the very region this chapter describes and diagnoses her people's worship in words that could describe this chapter's own verdict, you worship what you do not know, before announcing that true worship no longer depends on any mountain or temple at all.

Reports that Samaria had received the word of God, the first territory outside Judea to do so, and that the apostles themselves came to pray for the Spirit to fall on them, the New Testament's own answer to this chapter's tragic verdict that none of Samaria's residents truly worshiped the LORD.

study.oneStory:
This chapter is the theological hinge of the whole book of Kings, and one of the most important in the Old Testament's larger account of exile. Genesis already established that sin fractures a relationship with God into distance, a man and woman hiding from His presence among the trees; this chapter shows an entire nation finally removed from His presence, verses 18 and 23, the same rupture now enacted on a national scale, centuries in the making, after every possible warning had been offered and refused. Israel's fall previews, almost verse for verse, what will happen to Judah itself in the book's closing chapters, using nearly identical covenant curse language, so that this chapter functions as a warning Judah's own readers were meant to feel land on themselves before it ever did.

Yet judgment is never the whole of what this chapter records. Only the tribe of Judah remained, verse 18, a single surviving thread carrying forward the promise made to David, proof that even total national catastrophe cannot unravel what God Himself has determined to preserve. And the chapter's closing failure, a resettled people who worship the LORD without truly knowing Him, does not stay a failure forever. Centuries later, in the same towns and villages this chapter names, a woman at a well hears the truth about her own incomplete worship from the lips of the very Messiah that remnant of Judah was kept alive to produce, and not long after that, the whole region receives the word of God, Acts 8:14, becoming a testimony to the reach of a rescue this chapter could never have anticipated for a people it had just condemned. What begins here as a nation removed from God's presence ends, in the new creation, with His servants who will see His face, Revelation 22:4, presence restored beyond anything Samaria's exiled generation could have imagined possible for themselves or their conquerors.

quiz.q: What led directly to the king of Assyria's final siege and capture of Samaria?

options.text: Hoshea conspired with Egypt's king and stopped paying tribute to Assyria, prompting Assyria's king to imprison him and besiege the city for three years.
options.note: Verses 3 to 6 record this exact sequence of rebellion and its consequences.

options.text: Israel launched an unprovoked invasion of Assyrian territory.
options.note: The text describes Hoshea withholding tribute and seeking Egyptian alliance, not an Israelite invasion of Assyria.

options.text: Samaria surrendered voluntarily without any siege.
options.note: The text explicitly describes a three-year siege before the city's capture.

options.text: Assyria attacked without any prior provocation from Israel.
options.note: The text specifically attributes the invasion to Hoshea's rebellion and withheld tribute.

quiz.q: According to the author's theological explanation, what was the root cause of Israel's fall?

options.text: Centuries of persistent idolatry and covenant unfaithfulness, despite repeated warnings from the LORD's prophets, going back to the sins Jeroboam introduced.
options.note: Verses 7 to 23 give this extended, explicit explanation as the direct cause of the exile.

options.text: Simply poor military strategy and weak alliances.
options.note: The author's stated explanation is thoroughly theological and covenantal, not merely a commentary on military or political strategy.

options.text: The size and strength of the Assyrian empire alone.
options.note: While Assyria's power is the historical instrument, the author explicitly attributes the ultimate cause to Israel's own persistent sin.

options.text: The text gives no explanation for Israel's fall.
options.note: Verses 7 to 23 constitute one of the longest theological explanations in the entire book.

quiz.q: Why did the LORD send lions among the foreign peoples resettled in Samaria?

options.text: Because the new settlers did not worship the LORD, the God of the land they now inhabited.
options.note: Verse 25 gives this exact and explicit reason.

options.text: Because they had destroyed all the remaining Israelite shrines.
options.note: The text attributes the lions specifically to their failure to worship the LORD, not to destroying shrines.

options.text: Because they refused to pay tribute to the king of Assyria.
options.note: The lions are explicitly tied to religious failure to worship the LORD, not political tribute issues.

options.text: The lions are never explained in the text.
options.note: Verse 25 provides a clear, explicit explanation for this event.

quiz.q: How is the worship of the resettled peoples ultimately described at the end of the chapter?

options.text: They worshiped the LORD but also served their own idols according to their former customs, a divided worship the text explicitly says fails to count as truly worshiping the LORD.
options.note: Verses 33 to 34 and 41 record this exact, pointed description of mixed, divided worship.

options.text: They fully abandoned all their former gods and worshiped only the LORD.
options.note: The text explicitly states they continued serving their own gods alongside the LORD, not full abandonment of idolatry.

options.text: They rejected the LORD entirely and worshiped only their native gods.
options.note: The text specifically notes they did include some worship of the LORD, though incompletely and alongside idols.

options.text: No description of their worship practices is given.
options.note: Verses 24 to 41 give an extended and detailed description of their mixed worship practices.

quiz.q: What did the LORD's covenant specifically require of Israel regarding other gods, as restated in verses 35 to 39?

options.text: To worship the LORD exclusively, never bowing down to, serving, or sacrificing to any other god, since He alone had brought them out of Egypt.
options.note: Verses 35 to 39 restate this exact exclusive covenant demand in detail.

options.text: To worship the LORD as the primary god while permitting minor local deities.
options.note: The text explicitly and repeatedly forbids worship of any other god whatsoever, allowing no exceptions.

options.text: To worship whichever god seemed most powerful at any given time.
options.note: The covenant demand is fixed and exclusive to the LORD alone, not contingent on perceived power of rival gods.

options.text: The covenant made no specific demands regarding other gods.
options.note: Verses 35 to 39 give an extended, explicit, and repeated demand for exclusive worship of the LORD.

questions: The LORD sent prophet after prophet for over two centuries before judgment finally fell on Israel. Where has God's patience with a persistent pattern in your own life been far longer than you perhaps deserved, and how should that shape your response now?

Israel is repeatedly described as stiffening its neck, refusing correction it clearly understood. Where might you be resisting a correction from God that you know full well but have simply refused to heed?

The resettled peoples worshiped the LORD alongside their own gods, and the text explicitly says this did not count as true worship at all. Where in your own life might you be trying to include God alongside other ultimate loyalties rather than giving Him your undivided devotion?

This chapter functions as the author's own explanation for why history unfolded as it did, rather than leaving events to speak for themselves. How comfortable are you interpreting difficult seasons in your own life through the lens of Scripture's explanations rather than assuming they are random or meaningless?

Israel's fall traces back to one early compromise, Jeroboam's golden calves, that was never fully corrected for generations. What early compromise in your own life or family history might still be quietly shaping choices today if left unaddressed?

translationNotes.note: King So of Egypt is likely an abbreviation for a specific Egyptian ruler, possibly Osorkon, though the exact historical identification remains debated among scholars.

The specific locations of exile, Halah, Gozan by the Habor River, and the cities of the Medes, are independently attested regions within the Assyrian empire, corroborating the historical reliability of this account.

The mixed population resettled in Samaria, combined with the remaining Israelites and the returning priest's incomplete instruction, forms the historical and religious background for the later Samaritans of the New Testament, whose worship the Gospel of John describes as incomplete, John 4:20-22.
